findings.where: First screen, top bar (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: There is no navigation. The top bar holds only the name and the mark, so there is no way to reach articles, talks, a CV or a Contact label. The palette table even assigns a colour to 'nav links' that the page never shows.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer arriving from LinkedIn who wants to check Mark's work or publications before writing to him has nowhere to go but the one email address. The founder also asked for nav on the first screen.

findings.where: Blue band below the hero, 'Subscribe' button
findings.fault: The Subscribe button links to #subscribe, and nothing on the page has that anchor. The button does nothing.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who presses it expects to sign up, gets no response, and comes away thinking the site is broken or neglected.

findings.where: Blue band below the hero, 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform'
findings.fault: The band adds a second action, and in a squint it outweighs the hero's single email action: it is a full-bleed field in the house blue with a large heading, and it fills a whole screen on the phone. It also speaks of Mark in the third person in marketing phrasing, and it offers 'briefings' that no source shows Mark provides.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for one direct way to reach Mark, in his own voice, with no invented offers. The audience would also read the band as a salesy newsletter push from a firm rather than a personal advisor.

findings.where: Article specimen: body paragraphs, the subhead 'So, what are the key chapter topics?', the numbered list and the closing paragraph (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The body text is centred while the title, byline and caption are left-aligned. Every line of reading starts at a different point. In the list, the numbers hang at the left while the item text is centred, so each item drifts away from its number (item 2 starts far from its '2.').
findings.who_objects: Readers of Mark's long articles (bank and agency staff reading closely) lose their place at each line break. Angélique's real posts would all inherit the same hard-to-read setting.

findings.fault: The direction asks for Mark at work: a full-bleed photograph of him speaking, with the line set over its calm side. Here his backdrop is keyed out, leaving a large floating head and shoulders on a flat field. The lectern, the event and the room are all gone, so the hero reads as a cut-out portrait on a coloured ground. The keyed edge is also visibly rough around the crown and the right side of the head at 1440 px.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who chose this direction for its 'at work' context, and the audience, for whom a speaking engagement is itself evidence of standing. A head pasted onto navy reads as a campaign poster, not a working advisor.

findings.where: First screen, the name and logo lockup at top left
findings.fault: 'Mark M. Moseley' is set small and light beside a larger, bolder white aqueduct mark, so the firm's mark wins over his name.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose personal-advisor test asks that Mark's name lead with the logo beside it, not the other way round.

findings.where: First screen, the name 'Mark M. Moseley' in the top bar and the footer
findings.fault: The name sits in the position of a home link and draws its own box, but it does nothing. Only the mark beside it links home.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who clicks the name to return home, as on most personal sites, gets no response.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture card 'Streamlining the PPP Process…'
findings.fault: The card shows a download arrow and the label 'PDF', but the link goes to an in-page article anchor, not a file.
findings.who_objects: A reader who wants the lecture file to keep or forward expects a download and lands somewhere else.

findings.fault: It is the only element on the page with rounded corners, a blue tint, a blue border and a wide soft drop shadow, all at once. It reads like an app widget or a promotion dropped into an otherwise flat, square, editorial page.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for a refined look with no slickness. The audience may also read it as an ad rather than one of Mark's papers.

findings.fault: This label is set in the link blue, although the page's own rule is 'blue only where something can be clicked'. It is also in tracked capitals, which the type pair note rules out ('never tracked capitals').
findings.who_objects: A visitor who takes blue to mean a link tries to click it. The page also breaks its own stated rules in the first specimen.

findings.where: Specimen section labels: 'PALETTE', 'Type pair', 'Texture', 'An article page', 'Motion sketch'
findings.fault: Labels with the same role get three different treatments: blue tracked capitals, small bold grey sans, and a large italic serif for 'Texture' alone.
findings.who_objects: The founder, comparing tiles. The inconsistent labels make the specimen look unfinished and blur which parts are headings of the same rank.

findings.fault: This is a button, but it is styled as an underlined link, borrowing the link's reserved underline.
findings.who_objects: A keyboard or screen-reader user, or a careful visitor, expects it to navigate rather than replay the animation in place.

findings.where: First screen, the mark reversed to white on slate
findings.fault: The logo is shown in an all-white version the client has not supplied or approved.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo it is. A reversed version needs his yes before it can carry the site's first screen.

findings.where: First screen, the lede and the area around the action
findings.fault: The lede says what Mark does and for whom, but not where he has worked. Nothing near the email gives proof of his work: no named body that asked for it, no talk, no year.
findings.who_objects: A procurement-minded bank officer needs to see regions and evidence of comparable work before writing. Without them the first screen asks for contact on a statement alone.
